content: This study was commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO), and the authors have declared no conflicts of interest. Abbreviations Used: CI: Confidence Interval F-75: Therapeutic milk used during the stabilization phase of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) treatment F-100: Therapeutic milk used during the transition and recovery phases of SAM treatment IQR: Interquartile Range MUAC: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference NCHS: National Center for Health Statistics NGO: Non-Governmental Organization OTP: Outpatient Treatment Program PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes RCT: Randomized Controlled Trial RUTF: Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food SAM: Severe Acute Malnutrition SD: Standard Deviation SFP: Supplementary Feeding Programme W/H: Weight-for-Height WHM: Weight-for-Height Percentage of the Median WHO: World Health Organization WHO-GS: WHO Child Growth Standards WHZ: Weight-for-Height Z-Score Background: A low mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) of less than 115 mm is increasingly being used as a standalone criterion for admitting children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) into nutritional rehabilitation programs. This is alongside the traditional weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) of less than -3. However, these two indicators correlate poorly. This review aimed to evaluate the outcomes of children admitted and discharged from nutritional rehabilitation programs based on either MUAC or WHZ. The use of bilateral pitting edema as an independent indicator of SAM was not included in this review. Methods: The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases such as Medline, Embase, CRD, and the Cochrane Library, as well as grey literature, to identify evidence on mortality, recovery, treatment duration, costs, adverse events, and population coverage when SAM admissions were based on MUAC versus WHZ. Eleven studies were included in the review. Only one cohort study directly compared children with MUAC <115 mm and those with WHZ <-3 at the start of nutritional rehabilitation. This study found similar mortality rates between the two groups, although the causes of death may differ. Children with low MUAC were more likely to be stunted, younger, female, and have nutritional edema compared to those with low WHZ. Findings: Four studies admitted children based solely on MUAC. One study reported slower daily MUAC gains in younger, smaller children and females. Two studies discharged children based on MUAC thresholds (e.g., MUAC ≥124 mm or ≥130 mm) but did not report post-discharge outcomes. The optimal MUAC cut-off for discharge remains unknown. No studies reported on costs, adverse effects, or population coverage. Additionally, no studies assessed the outcomes of children with low WHZ who were excluded from treatment because they did not meet the MUAC-only admission criteria. Conclusion: There is evidence suggesting that MUAC could be used as a standalone criterion for admitting and discharging children with SAM from nutritional rehabilitation programs. However, the current evidence base is insufficient. More data are needed, particularly on the risks faced by children with low WHZ who are not treated for SAM when MUAC is used as the sole criterion. Additionally, the influence of factors such as age, sex, and stunting on rehabilitation outcomes in children admitted with MUAC <115 mm needs further clarification. Thorough evaluations of existing nutritional programs worldwide could provide valuable data in the short term. Background and Objective: In 1999, the WHO defined severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6–59 months as a weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) below -3 standard deviations (SD) or the presence of bilateral pitting edema. The reference population used was the 1978 NCHS reference until the release of the 2006 WHO Child Growth Standards (WHO-GS). In 2007, United Nations agencies endorsed a low MUAC (<110 mm) as an independent diagnostic criterion for SAM, alongside WHZ <-3 or nutritional edema. This cut-off was later increased to MUAC <115 mm to better align with the WHZ <-3 classification under the 2006 WHO-GS. This makes it suitable for large community-based programs, even in resource-limited settings. Since its endorsement, MUAC has been increasingly used as a standalone admission criterion for nutritional rehabilitation in countries such as Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and Pakistan. However, MUAC and WHZ-based diagnoses of malnutrition correlate poorly, with only about 40% of children identified as SAM by one indicator also diagnosed as such by the other. This discrepancy poses significant programmatic challenges. Relying on only one indicator may under-detect true cases of acute malnutrition, while using both indicators could inflate program volumes unnecessarily. Additionally, the choice of anthropometric indicator for monitoring recovery and deciding discharge remains unclear. Research Questions: The review aimed to address the following questions: 1. Can MUAC be used as a standalone criterion for SAM diagnosis, monitoring recovery, and discharge? 2. What are the short-term mortality rates, recovery rates, time to recovery, weight/MUAC/length gains, resource use, costs, adverse effects, and population coverage when MUAC is used compared to WHZ? Results: The review retrieved 326 references, with 12 papers reporting on 11 studies meeting the inclusion criteria. Five studies used MUAC as a standalone criterion for admitting children into nutritional rehabilitation programs. The remaining six studies admitted children based on low WHZ but reported on MUAC gains during rehabilitation. Most studies were conducted in African countries, with five taking place in Malawi. The majority treated uncomplicated SAM cases in outpatient settings. No randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing outcomes of children admitted based on low WHZ versus low MUAC were found. Only one observational study, conducted in Kenya, compared mortality risk in hospitalized children based on MUAC versus WHZ levels. This study reported similar mortality rates but noted differences in clinical profiles between the two groups. Children with low MUAC were more likely to have kwashiorkor, stunting, and be younger and female compared to those with low WHZ. Discussion: Direct evidence comparing treatment outcomes of SAM children diagnosed by MUAC versus WHZ is scarce. The available evidence suggests that children with low MUAC respond to nutritional rehabilitation in terms of weight and MUAC gains, although recovery rates were low in some studies. Children admitted with lower MUAC displayed greater daily MUAC gains during rehabilitation. However, no studies assessed outcomes after discharge when MUAC was used as the discharge criterion. The findings indicate that MUAC could be used as a standalone criterion for diagnosing, monitoring, and discharging SAM children. However, critical evidence gaps remain, particularly regarding the outcomes of children with WHZ <-3 who are excluded from treatment because their MUAC is ≥115 mm. Additionally, the optimal MUAC cut-off for discharge and the influence of factors such as age, sex, and stunting on rehabilitation outcomes need further investigation. Conclusion: While MUAC shows promise as a standalone criterion for SAM management, the evidence base is currently insufficient to make strong recommendations.
